name: Shabbetai Tzvi
bio: Shabbetai Tzvi (commonly dated 1 August 1626–17 September 1676; also Sabbatai Zevi and Turkish Sabatay Sevi) was an Ottoman Jewish mystic whose messianic claims generated the transregional Sabbatean movement. Born in Smyrna to the prosperous merchant Mordecai Tzvi, he received a traditional Talmudic education and immersed himself in Kabbalah. Periods of ascetic withdrawal alternated with public, deliberately transgressive “strange acts”; modern psychiatric descriptions remain retrospective interpretations, not diagnoses. After opposition drove him from Smyrna, he travelled among Salonica, Constantinople, Cairo and Jerusalem. His decisive encounter with Nathan of Gaza in 1665 transformed intermittent self-identification into a coordinated messianic campaign. Letters and rumours spread through Jewish communities from Yemen and Persia to North Africa and northern Europe, producing repentance, prophetic enthusiasm, suspended fasts and bitter communal division. Ottoman authorities arrested him in 1666. At Edirne he converted to Islam as Aziz Mehmed Efendi, receiving an imperial stipend. Most adherents abandoned him, but others interpreted apostasy as part of redemption; Tzvi continued an ambiguous Jewish-Muslim religious life until renewed Ottoman suspicion brought exile to Dulcigno, now Ulcinj, in 1673. His death did not end Sabbateanism: secret believers, the Ottoman Dönme and later movements including Frankism reworked its theology for generations.

name: Edmond James de Rothschild
bio: Edmond James de Rothschild (19 August 1845–2 November 1934), widely remembered in Israel as Baron Rothschild or HaNadiv HaYadua, was a French Jewish financier, collector, scientific patron and the principal private sponsor of many First Aliyah agricultural settlements. Born at Boulogne-Billancourt to James Mayer de Rothschild and Betty von Rothschild, he entered the Paris family bank, served France during the Franco-Prussian War and married Adelheid von Rothschild in 1877. After meeting Samuel Mohilever and representatives of struggling settlers in 1882, he financed land, water, housing, schools, health services, vineyards and industries in Ottoman Palestine. Rishon LeZion, Zikhron Ya’akov, Rosh Pina and numerous other colonies survived or expanded through his support. His administrators also imposed centralized control, provoking prolonged disputes with farmers over labour, crops and autonomy. In 1899–1900 he transferred direct administration to the Jewish Colonization Association; in 1924 he reorganized its Palestine branch as PICA under his son James. Initially wary of Theodor Herzl’s public political strategy, Rothschild later cooperated with Zionist leaders and advocated a Jewish national future. In France he supported scientific institutes, archaeology and the arts, leaving the Louvre more than 40,000 prints, nearly 3,000 drawings and hundreds of illustrated books. His settlement programme shaped the Yishuv’s agricultural and institutional geography, while its paternalism remains essential to evaluating that legacy.
title: French Jewish philanthropist, art collector and patron of settlement in Ottoman Palestine
aliases: Abraham Edmond Benjamin James de Rothschild
אברהם בנימין אדמונד ג׳יימס דה רוטשילד

name: Israel Zangwill
bio: Israel Zangwill (21 January 1864–1 August 1926) was a British Jewish novelist, playwright, journalist and political activist. Born in London to impoverished immigrants from the Russian Empire, he spent part of his childhood in Plymouth and Bristol before attending—and later teaching at—the Jews’ Free School in London’s East End. His 1892 novel Children of the Ghetto made him an influential interpreter of immigrant Jewish life, while The King of Schnorrers, Dreamers of the Ghetto and other fiction explored tradition, assimilation and modernity through comedy and social criticism. His 1908 play The Melting Pot popularized that metaphor for American immigrant integration. Zangwill met Theodor Herzl in London in 1895, helped introduce political Zionism to a British audience and attended the First Zionist Congress. After the Seventh Congress rejected the East Africa proposal in 1905, he founded the Jewish Territorial Organization, seeking an autonomous refuge wherever practicable for Jews endangered by persecution. The movement investigated territories on several continents and helped sponsor the Galveston immigration program, but secured no autonomous homeland. Zangwill briefly re-engaged with mainstream Zionism after the Balfour Declaration, then renewed his territorialist criticism. Married to novelist and suffrage activist Edith Ayrton, he also campaigned for women’s suffrage, racial equality and—especially during the First World War—peace. His legacy joins Anglo-Jewish literature with the competing Jewish national projects of his era.

name: Janusz Korczak
bio: Janusz Korczak, born Henryk Goldszmit (22 July 1878 or 1879–5 or 6 August 1942), was a Polish Jewish physician, educator, writer and children’s-rights theorist. Raised in Warsaw, he studied medicine and served as an army doctor before practising paediatrics at the Bersohn and Bauman Children’s Hospital. From 1912 he directed Dom Sierot, a Jewish orphanage created with Stefania Wilczyńska, and later helped shape Nasz Dom for Polish children. These were experimental self-governing communities: children participated in a parliament, peer court and newspaper, while adults were required to respect children as present persons rather than future adults. Korczak developed this practice in How to Love a Child and The Child’s Right to Respect, and explored authority, justice and childhood in fiction including King Matt the First and Kaytek the Wizard. He founded Mały Przegląd, an innovative newspaper substantially written and edited by children, and broadcast as the ‘Old Doctor.’ A Polish Jew with a consciously double cultural attachment, he visited Mandatory Palestine twice and studied kibbutz education without emigrating. Under German occupation he remained responsible for Dom Sierot after its forced removal into the Warsaw Ghetto, securing food and maintaining education while writing a diary. During the August 1942 deportation, Korczak and his colleagues accompanied approximately two hundred children to the Umschlagplatz and Treblinka, where all were murdered. Specific stories that German officers formally offered him release vary and cannot be treated as established fact; his documented decision not to abandon the children is sufficient to explain his enduring moral authority.

name: Albert Einstein
bio: Albert Einstein (14 March 1879–18 April 1955) was a German-born Jewish theoretical physicist whose work transformed modern physics. Raised in a largely secular Jewish family in Ulm and Munich, he was educated in Aarau and at the Swiss Federal Polytechnic in Zürich. While employed at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern, his four celebrated papers of 1905 explained the photoelectric effect, supplied decisive statistical evidence for atoms, established special relativity and derived mass–energy equivalence. He completed general relativity in Berlin in 1915; the theory’s successful eclipse test made him internationally famous in 1919. The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics recognized his theoretical work, particularly the law of the photoelectric effect. Einstein also made foundational contributions to quantum theory, statistical mechanics, stimulated emission and Bose–Einstein statistics, although he later challenged quantum mechanics’ probabilistic interpretation. Nazism and antisemitism drove him from Germany in 1933 to the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. A pacifist for much of his life, he nevertheless signed the 1939 Einstein–Szilard letter warning President Franklin D. Roosevelt about a possible German atomic bomb; afterward he campaigned for arms control and world government. Einstein supported cultural Zionism and the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, while advocating Arab–Jewish cooperation. He declined Israel’s presidency in 1952 and bequeathed his literary estate to the Hebrew University.

name: Sarah Schenirer
bio: Sarah Schenirer (15 July 1883–1 March 1935) was a Polish Jewish educator, writer and organizer who founded the Bais Yaakov movement for Orthodox girls. Born into a Hasidic family in Kraków, she completed eight years of Polish schooling but received no comparable formal Jewish education; she studied Yiddish religious texts independently while working as a seamstress. As a wartime refugee in Vienna, Schenirer encountered German neo-Orthodox teaching, especially sermons by Moshe David Flesch, which strengthened her resolve to address the religious alienation of traditionally raised girls educated in secular schools. Returning to Kraków, she organized women and in 1917 opened a supplementary class for twenty-five girls in her apartment. It was not history’s first Jewish girls’ school, but it became the model for an unusually extensive Orthodox system. Kraków Agudath Israel adopted the school in 1919; national sponsorship, Leo Deutschlander’s pedagogical support and Schenirer’s organizing journeys then helped the network expand across Poland. She founded a teachers’ seminary in 1923 and helped inspire Bnos Agudath Israel for graduates. Schenirer wrote Yiddish textbooks, memoirs, articles and plays that joined religious instruction with accessible storytelling. She did not present her project as feminist reform and emphasized traditional family roles, yet her schools created unprecedented educational and professional opportunities for Orthodox women. By her death from tuberculosis, Bais Yaakov had become a mass movement whose graduates later rebuilt schools internationally after the Holocaust.

name: David Ben-Gurion
bio: David Ben-Gurion (born David Grün; 16 October 1886–1 December 1973) was a Labor Zionist leader, principal founder of the State of Israel and its first prime minister. Raised in a Hebrew- and Zionist-oriented family in Płońsk, he immigrated to Ottoman Palestine in 1906, worked in agricultural settlements and became an organizer, journalist and advocate of Hebrew labour. Exiled during the First World War, he organized Zionist activity in New York, married Paula Munweis and joined the Jewish Legion. Under the British Mandate he helped found Ahdut HaAvoda, became the Histadrut’s first secretary-general, led Mapai and chaired the Jewish Agency Executive. On 14 May 1948 he proclaimed Israel’s independence and directed the government during the 1948 war. His insistence on a unified state army—including the Altalena confrontation and dissolution of independent commands—was central to state consolidation but remains contested. As prime minister and defence minister in 1948–1954 and 1955–1963, he oversaw mass immigration, austerity, West German reparations, the 1956 Sinai campaign and development of national institutions, while Israel’s Palestinian Arab citizens remained under military government for most of his premiership. His responsibility for policies during the Palestinian displacement of 1948 remains a major subject of historical debate. After bitter disputes over the Lavon Affair, he left Mapai, founded Rafi and eventually retired to Sde Boker. His writings, diaries and correspondence form a major documentary record of Zionism and early Israel.

name: Viktor Frankl
bio: Viktor Emil Frankl (26 March 1905–2 September 1997) was an Austrian Jewish neurologist, psychiatrist and philosopher who founded logotherapy and existential analysis, a meaning-centred school of psychotherapy. His central ideas did not originate in the concentration camps: while studying medicine in Vienna, he corresponded with Sigmund Freud, participated in Alfred Adler’s circle, published on psychotherapy and values, used the term ‘logotherapy’ by 1926 and organized free counselling for suicidal young people. Under Nazi rule he directed neurology at Vienna’s Rothschild Hospital, where he sometimes falsified diagnoses to protect psychiatric patients from the euthanasia programme. Deported with his family in 1942, he worked in psychological care at Theresienstadt and survived Auschwitz transit, Kaufering III and Türkheim; his parents, brother and first wife were murdered or died in the Holocaust. Returning to Vienna in 1945, Frankl reconstructed The Doctor and the Soul and dictated the camp memoir later titled Man’s Search for Meaning. As director of the Vienna Neurological Policlinic and a University of Vienna professor, he developed logotherapy through books and international teaching. Frankl argued that people retain responsibility for how they answer unavoidable circumstances and may discover meaning through work, love or their stance toward inescapable suffering. This claim was not an endorsement of preventable suffering, nor a theory that victims were responsible for persecution. His Jewish life included a bar mitzvah, Holocaust communal service and a second bar mitzvah in Jerusalem in 1988, while his published psychology was deliberately universal in scope.

name: Anne Frank
bio: Annelies Marie ‘Anne’ Frank (12 June 1929–February 1945) was a German-born Jewish diarist and Holocaust victim. Born in Frankfurt am Main, she fled Nazi Germany with her family and settled in Amsterdam in 1934. German occupation transformed her childhood through anti-Jewish registration, exclusion from ordinary school, compulsory identification and the threat of deportation. On her thirteenth birthday Anne received the red-checked notebook in which she began recording friendships, family tensions, persecution and her ambitions as a writer. After her sister Margot received a labour summons, the family entered a concealed annex behind Otto Frank’s business at 263 Prinsengracht on 6 July 1942. Eight people lived there for more than two years, entirely dependent on helpers who endangered themselves to obtain food, news and supplies. Inspired by a 1944 radio appeal to preserve wartime documents, Anne began revising her diary as a prospective book titled Het Achterhuis (The Secret Annex). The hiding place was raided on 4 August 1944; no theory identifying a betrayer has been proved. Anne was deported through Westerbork to Auschwitz-Birkenau and then Bergen-Belsen, where she and Margot probably died of typhus in February 1945. Miep Gies preserved Anne’s papers, and Otto Frank, the family’s sole survivor, compiled their surviving versions for publication in 1947. Forensic and textual research has conclusively authenticated Anne’s manuscripts. Her diary is both an unusually accomplished adolescent work and one individual testimony within the murder of six million Jews.

name: Chaim Weizmann
bio: Zionist leader, chemist, diplomat, first President of Israel, and key architect of the Balfour Declaration.

name: Heinrich Heine
bio: German Jewish poet, journalist, and literary critic, known for his lyric poetry and essays.

name: Sir Moses Haim Montefiore
bio: British financier, philanthropist, activist, Sheriff of London, and leading Jewish communal figure. President of the Board of Deputies of British Jews (1835–1874). A pivotal figure in Proto-Zionism; founded Mishkenot Sha'ananim (1860), the first Jewish neighborhood outside Jerusalem’s Old City.

name: Solomon Schechter
bio: Scholar and rabbinic leader. Famous for his work on the Cairo Geniza and as the second President of the Jewish Theological Seminary of America.

name: Theodor Herzl
bio: Theodor Herzl (1860–1904) was an Austro-Hungarian journalist, playwright, and political activist, widely regarded as the father of modern political Zionism. Trained in law and active as a correspondent and writer, he became convinced that the Jewish people could only ensure their security and dignity through the establishment of a sovereign Jewish state. His pamphlet 'Der Judenstaat' (1896) laid out this vision, and he went on to organize the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897, becoming the first President of the World Zionist Organization. Herzl tirelessly lobbied European leaders and Ottoman officials for support until his death in 1904.
